In [[geometry]] and [[topology]], '''trivial cylinders''' are certain [[pseudoholomorphic curve]]s appearing in certain cylindrical [[manifold]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hutchings |first=Micheal |date=2 November 2000 |title= An index inequality for embedded pseudoholomorphic curves in symplectizations|url=https://math.berkeley.edu/~hutching/pub/pfh2/pfh2published.pdf |journal= Journal of the European Mathematical Society|volume=4 |issue=4 |pages=313–361 |doi=10.1007/s100970100041 |via=University of Berkeley}}</ref>

In [[Floer homology]] and its variants, chain complexes or differential graded algebras are generated by certain combinations of closed orbits of [[vector fields]].  In symplectic Floer homology, one considers the [[Hamiltonian vector field]] of a Hamiltonian function on a [[symplectic manifold]]; in [[Symplectic geometry|symplectic field theory]], [[contact homology]], and their variants, one considers the [[Reeb vector field]] associated to a [[contact form]], or more generally a [[Hamiltonian (control theory)|stable Hamiltonian structure]].

The differentials all count some flavor of [[pseudoholomorphic curve]]s in a manifold with a cylindrical almost-complex structure whose ends at negative infinity are the given collection of closed orbits.  For instance, in symplectic Floer homology, one considers the product of the mapping torus of a symplectomorphism with the real numbers; in symplectic field theory, one considers the symplectization of a contact manifold.

The product of a given embedded closed orbit with R is always a pseudoholomorphic curve, and such a curve is called a ''trivial cylinder''.  Trivial cylinders do not generally contribute to the aforementioned differentials, but they may appear as components of more complicated curves which do.
